JSON: Name: echo_vision_fm_pipeline Title: Self-supervised masked-autoencoding pretraining with a spatial-temporal fusion network for end-to-end echocardiogram video analysis Short Hypothesis: Pretraining a ViT-based video encoder on large-scale unlabeled echocardiogram videos using high-ratio masked autoencoding and fine-tuning it with an inserted Spatial-Temporal Fusion Network (STF-Net) will reduce LV ejection fraction regression MAE and increase diagnostic AUC on external echocardiogram test sets compared to (a) the same encoder trained from random initialization and (b) the same encoder fine-tuned without STF-Net. Related Work: Prior approaches to automated echocardiogram analysis fall into two broad families: multi-stage segmentation pipelines that first predict frame-level masks and then derive clinical metrics via rule-based post-processing, and end-to-end video or frame-based models that directly regress or classify outcomes. Segmentation pipelines yield interpretable intermediate outputs but require large annotation budgets and can accumulate errors across stages; they also typically operate on single frames or selected frames rather than full video dynamics. Video-focused methods (3D CNNs, two-stream networks, and transformer-based video encoders) capture temporal patterns but previous variants often require large supervised labels or were pre-trained on non-medical video corpora, limiting transferability. Self-supervised strategies (contrastive learning, masked autoencoding) have shown promise for reducing annotation needs, but applications to echocardiography have been limited by dataset scale, the temporal redundancy of cardiac video, and insufficient fusion mechanisms to fully exploit complementary spatial and temporal signals. Existing methods rarely evaluate generalization across multiple independent clinical cohorts or quantify the impact of pretraining mask ratio, pretraining data volume, and fusion architectures in a controlled ablation. Abstract: We present a reproducible research pipeline that tests whether self-supervised masked-autoencoding pretraining on large-scale unlabeled echocardiogram videos, combined with a compact Spatial-Temporal Fusion Network (STF-Net) inserted before task heads, improves end-to-end cardiac function and disease prediction. The pipeline uses a ViT-based video encoder pretrained with an 85% token-mask ratio on a public MIMIC-IV-ECHO corpus to learn joint spatiotemporal features without manual labels. After discarding the lightweight decoder, the pre-trained encoder is fine-tuned on downstream clinical tasks using the full video clip as input; STF-Net aggregates and fuses learned spatial and temporal feature maps through dual pathways (joint and disjoint) prior to prediction. The main contribution is a complete experimental protocol that quantifies transferability, data-efficiency, and the incremental value of STF-Net by evaluating LV ejection fraction regression, LV volume estimation, and disease severity classification across external datasets. Expected outcomes are lower regression errors, higher AUCs, and clearer empirical guidance on mask ratio, pretraining size, and fusion design for medical video foundation models. Experiments: Pretraining: dataset: MIMIC-IV-ECHO (≈525k echocardiogram videos). Input preprocessing: uniformly sample T=16 frames per clip, resize to 3x224x224, cube-embedding with τ=2, h=w=16, representation dimension d=768. Pretraining objective: Video masked auto-encoder (VideoMAE variant), mask ratio sweep [50,70,80,85,90] with primary value 85%. Optimizer: AdamW (β1=0.9, β2=0.95), weight decay=0.05, cosine LR with peak=1e-4, warmup first 5% (initial LR=1e-5), epochs=30, batch=8, mixed precision; run on A100 GPUs; repeat each config 3 seeds. Downstream datasets and splits: EchoNet-Dynamic (10,030 videos) train/val/test per official split; CAMUS (500 exams; 450 train/50 test); TMED/TMED-2 (599 AS cases) use provided labels and official splits. Downstream tasks and metrics: LV EF regression — MAE (%), RMSE (pp), R^2; LV ESV/EDV regression — MAE (ml), R^2; binary heart-function classification (EF<50%) — AUC, accuracy, F1; aortic stenosis multi-class classification — AUC (macro), accuracy, F1; CAMUS per-subject LV EF — Pearson correlation, mean bias, standard deviation. Baselines: (1) same ViT video encoder randomly initialized; (2) ViT pretrained via publicly available VideoMAE on generic video or ImageNet-initialized ViT; (3) VideoResNet pretrained on same subsets; (4) ViViT pretrained; (5) segmentation-based pipelines using UNet/Swin-UNet/H2Former + Simpson post-processing; (6) end-to-end prior video models. Fine-tuning setup: freeze encoder for linear-probing experiments and unfreeze for full fine-tuning; optimizer AdamW (β1=0.9, β2=0.98), weight decay=1e-3, cosine LR decay, batch=16, epochs=50; choose best checkpoint by validation loss; run 3 seeds. Ablations and comparisons: (A) with vs without STF-Net (inserted between encoder output and task head) across all downstream tasks; (B) mask ratio sweep during pretraining [50,70,80,85,90] evaluated on EchoNet-Dynamic EF regression; (C) pretraining-data fraction ablation [25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of MIMIC-IV-ECHO] with both linear-probing and full fine-tuning; (D) encoder initialization variants (random, VideoMAE, full echocardiogram pretraining) to isolate pretraining benefit; (E) low-data fine-tuning regimes [1%, 10%, 100%] for downstream tasks to quantify data-efficiency. Statistical reporting: mean±std over seeds, paired statistical significance tests (two-sided t-test) with threshold p<0.05 comparing primary model (pretrained + STF-Net) vs best baseline. Operational metrics: inference latency per 16-frame clip (ms) on single A100, GPU memory footprint (GB) during inference. Expected reproducible outputs: full training logs, saved checkpoints, and evaluation scripts. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Dataset bias and domain shift: MIMIC-IV-ECHO and downstream public datasets may not represent global device vendors, acquisition protocols, patient demographics, or rare pathologies, limiting external validity. 2) Temporal information loss: frame sampling (T=16) and high mask ratios exploit redundancy but can omit fine temporal motion details needed for some diagnoses, degrading performance on rapid or subtle motion phenomena. 3) Mask-ratio sensitivity: excessively high masking (>85%) can harm transferability; optimal mask ratio may vary by downstream task and dataset. 4) Annotation noise and label variability: ground-truth EF and volume measurements have inter-observer variance and measurement error, which inflate apparent model error and complicate comparisons. 5) Compute and reproducibility limits: full pretraining requires multi-day A100-class GPU resources and storage for hundreds of thousands of videos, restricting replication. 6) Failure modes: models may attend to dataset-specific confounders (machine overlays, view labels, ECG traces) rather than anatomy, producing non-robust predictors. 7) Generalization to other views/modalities: the pipeline is validated primarily on apical views and TTE; performance on other echocardiographic views, transesophageal studies, or non-echocardiographic 3D modalities (CT/MRI) is unknown. 8) Clinical deployment constraints: retrospective performance does not guarantee prospective clinical utility; regulatory, interpretability, and integration requirements are not addressed. 9) Evaluation limitations: public test sets are limited in size (e.g., CAMUS=50 test cases), leading to wider confidence intervals for some metrics.
